Investigate treams autodiff without requiring users to import backend-specific treams modules.

This is a separate, non-blocking design investigation requested by the repository owner during release preparation. The release agent continues independently. Do not contact the release agent or wait for release work. Do not implement changes now.

The user's question was: "is it possible to make autodiff work for treams with different autodiff backends with importing specific treams autodiff backends? right now having to do import treams.advect is somewhat unintuitive". Interpret this as asking whether the ordinary treams API can select the appropriate differentiation adapter WITHOUT imports such as import treams.advect, while retaining Advect, JAX, and PyTorch support.

Authoritative source:

  • treams-rs, release/integration at fcf62400700e326ffcc61ec50025cb25ea43ea6d. Recheck the revision, and use git show at that SHA if release work later advances it.
  • advect, currently d5f4bae154f040f1e80c32dc7c1aab41e4c155dc. Recheck the revision and inspect current code rather than assuming old architecture.

Constraints:

  • Read-only investigation. Do not edit either repository, add dependencies, create worktrees, run native builds, change Git refs, commit, push, open issues/PRs, or send external messages.
  • No dependency installation or broad test suites. Small existing-environment probes are fine if they do not rebuild/install anything. Cap CPU threads at 1 for any probe. If relevant environments are unavailable, use source evidence and state the execution gap.
  • Do not modify Codex or user configuration, memories, or agent skills. Do not inspect credentials.
  • Final answer is the durable report; the launcher writes it outside the repository. Include exact source file/line pointers and revision IDs. Do not attempt to write files yourself in the read-only sandbox.
  • Prefer the smallest coherent design. New registries, plugin systems, compatibility layers, elaborate fallback paths, and global state need a concrete reason.
  • Prose must be objective, concise, approachable, and respectful of the reader's time. Explain necessary programming terms briefly. Physics terminology is fine.

Questions to resolve:

  1. What do the existing treams modules and backends actually expose, and what prevents ordinary treams calls from preserving differentiation today? Distinguish Python class methods, ufunc-like functions, raw NumPy operations, and Rust calls. Establish the correct import namespace (treams_rs vs treams) from source.
  2. Can selection by input array/tracer types transparently reuse the existing custom derivative implementations? Cover Advect tracing, JAX tracing and JIT, PyTorch eager and compile, array_ufunc, array_function, array_namespace/Array API. Explain why a protocol is or is not sufficient at the Rust derivative boundary.
  3. How can optional backend imports stay lazy and avoid startup cost/mandatory dependencies? Preserve ordinary NumPy return types and behavior. Identify ambiguity with Python floats/NumPy arrays, zero differentiable inputs, nested containers, constructors and materials, constants, mixed backend values, tracing-context detection, and accidental array coercions.
  4. Compare a small transparent dispatch boundary with one explicit backend/context choice and the existing modules. Recommend the smallest useful supported scope. Do not imply a universal implementation is already present.
  5. Provide a short proposed user-facing API example that can be run after implementation, clearly labeled as a proposal; separately show an existing runnable equivalent where possible. Include realistic gradients/parameters rather than invented function names. State JIT/compile/higher-order/device limits based on current adapters.
  6. Outline the minimal implementation locations and meaningful validation needed for a later change, including output/cotangent conventions and performance of ordinary NumPy calls. No implementation in this investigation.

Check current official library documentation if needed for changing or uncertain external API claims. Use primary sources only and cite exact pages. Local repository source is authoritative for project-specific behavior. […]

Deliver a concise decision first, then evidence, alternatives/tradeoffs, and a bounded follow-up plan. Clearly separate source-confirmed facts, inferences, and behavior not executed. This report must not create a release blocker.

This app-server thread replaces the initial non-interactive CLI session [A first try at gradient frameworks] so that the investigation can be found in the ordinary thread list. Reuse its source excerpts and searches from release workspace: followups/autodiff-imports/events.jsonl. If release workspace: followups/autodiff-imports/report.md already exists, review that report instead of repeating its investigation. The prior CLI session is being stopped after this thread starts. The launcher will save YOUR final report to release workspace: followups/autodiff-imports/app-thread-report.md; do not write that path yourself.

The prior session left source excerpts but no finished report, and both checkouts still match the supplied revisions. The main issue is now clear: ordinary calls convert inputs to NumPy or Python scalars and discard derivative contexts; the existing adapters preserve them. Automatic selection must happen before those conversions.

items.html:
Yes—ordinary treams_rs calls can select the existing Advect, JAX, or PyTorch adapter from their inputs. The derivatives already exist. The missing work is dispatch before conversions lose tracing information, plus consistent handling of constant physics objects.

I recommend a bounded follow-up: support sphere_tmatrix(...) and its scattering calculation through the ordinary API first. Preserve NumPy behavior for NumPy inputs, reuse the existing adapters, and avoid a new plugin registry or global backend setting. This is not a release blocker.

Both supplied revisions were verified:

  • treams-rs: fcf62400700e326ffcc61ec50025cb25ea43ea6d, on release/integration.
  • Advect: d5f4bae154f040f1e80c32dc7c1aab41e4c155dc.

All project-source pointers below refer to those revisions, inspected using git show. The prior session’s excerpts were reused; no completed report.md existed.

What exists today

The import namespace is treams_rs, not treams. The latter is the upstream project whose API this package follows. The root package explicitly documents its NumPy behavior and separate differentiation namespaces. Root API

Surface Current behavior
Root Python factories and class methods Construct NumPy physics objects. For example, TMatrix.sphere constructs ordinary materials, calls diff.sphere, and discards its derivative context. Source
special, wave and lattice functions A mixture of actual NumPy ufuncs, Python wrappers, and native functions. Their contracts include broadcasting, scalar fast paths, and sometimes out/where; they are not one uniform dispatch surface. Source
diff Explicit value-plus-context operations. A context’s pullback maps an output gradient to input gradients. Contract
advect, jax, torch Existing custom derivative bridges and shared framework physics objects, bound to different execution backends. Shared constructors

The barriers are concrete: root Material calls complex(...); frequency validation returns float(...); physics arrays store NumPy copies. Depending on the framework, these conversions can reject traced values or lose their derivative connection. Even successfully reaching Rust does not register a derivative: its sphere binding accepts concrete f64/NumPy arrays and returns a value plus a context. Material, frequency, physics arrays, Rust boundary

Why input dispatch works—and protocols alone do not

A dispatcher can recognize Advect tracers, JAX arrays/tracers, or PyTorch tensors, then call the corresponding existing constructor. Returned framework objects already retain their backend for subsequent methods.

For Advect, use public advect.is_traced(value), rather than depending on one tracer class. It checks a value without reading its payload; nested containers need separate inspection. Importantly, Advect’s NumPy tracer returns the NumPy namespace from __array_namespace__, so namespace selection alone cannot identify differentiation. Recognition, namespace

The protocols solve different problems:

  • __array_ufunc__ intercepts NumPy ufunc calls; __array_function__ intercepts participating NumPy functions. Neither automatically intercepts arbitrary Python class methods or supplies a derivative for an opaque Rust kernel. Advect implements both, but a foreign operation still needs a derivative rule. NumPy documentation, Advect implementation
  • __array_namespace__ supplies an array-operation namespace. It does not standardize custom derivatives, saved contexts, or compiler integration. It can help with surrounding arithmetic, but cannot replace these adapters. Array API specification
  • Raw NumPy operations are only differentiable where the selected framework supports their interception. Dispatch inside treams cannot make arbitrary caller-side NumPy code traceable. JAX, for example, documents errors from converting tracers to NumPy. JAX documentation

The existing bridges are therefore the right boundary: Advect uses a primitive with a saved pullback; JAX uses custom_vjp and host callbacks; PyTorch uses autograd.Function. Advect, JAX, PyTorch

The main design issue is constants

This apparently simple proposal is incomplete:

sphere = tr.sphere_tmatrix(radius=traced_radius, ...)
wave = tr.plane_wave([0, 0, 1], ...)
sphere.cross_sections(wave)

The sphere could select a framework, while the all-constant wave remains a NumPy object. Those classes currently do not compose: the framework code calls in_basis(..., positions=..., singular=False), whereas the root plane wave accepts only basis. Framework consumer, root method

A minimal transparent design therefore needs these rules:

  • No backend-bearing inputs: retain the existing NumPy path and return types. Python floats and NumPy arrays cannot reveal an intended backend, even inside a differentiated function.
  • One backend: select it before coercion; convert numeric constants through that adapter. Recognize tensors even when requires_grad=False.
  • Constant physics objects: narrowly promote supported objects, initially an incident NumPy plane wave, when a framework object consumes them.
  • Nested values: inspect supported lists, tuples, and material fields before array construction. Avoid arbitrary object traversal or object-array discovery.
  • Materials: initially accept differentiated epsilon or material tuples directly. Supporting tr.Material(traced_epsilon) requires dispatch before its complex(...) conversion; later promotion cannot recover a lost trace.
  • Mixed frameworks: raise a clear error before conversion. Do not silently detach or select whichever input appears first.
  • Tracing context: do not infer a backend from installed/imported packages or ambient “gradient enabled” state. Advect’s direct tracing query is private, and context detection does not resolve multiple active frameworks. Advect context

Lazy loading is straightforward in principle: consult already-loaded framework modules and their public recognition APIs, then import only the selected treams adapter. The root package already lazily loads optional namespaces and reports missing dependencies. Plain NumPy calls should never import them. This dispatch strategy is a proposal, not existing functionality. Current lazy loader

Alternatives and recommendation

Choice Tradeoff
Existing tr.advect, tr.jax, tr.torch Smallest solution today; consistent handling of constants, but requires explicit selection.
One explicit backend-bound API Resolves constant-only construction without ambient state. Existing namespaces already provide this; another selector adds little.
Backend context manager Covers constant constructors, but introduces implicit state and JIT trace-time semantics. Unnecessary initially.
Transparent input dispatch Best match for the requested ordinary API; requires bounded constant promotion and documented coverage.

Recommend transparent dispatch for the named sphere factory and cross-section workflow across all three adapters. Keep class constructors such as TMatrix.sphere, arbitrary root methods, and low-level ufunc replacement outside that first change. Replacing genuine ufuncs with ordinary wrappers would require separately preserving their methods, broadcasting and out/where contracts.

Proposed user experience—requires implementation

import numpy as np
import advect as ad
import treams_rs as tr

def scattering(parameters):
    radius, epsilon = parameters
    sphere = tr.sphere_tmatrix(
        k0=2.0, lmax=2, radius=radius, material=epsilon
    )
    wave = tr.plane_wave([0, 0, 1], "positive_helicity", k0=2.0)
    return sphere.cross_sections(wave).scattering

value, gradient = ad.value_and_grad(scattering)(np.array([0.2, 3.0]))
# gradient contains derivatives with respect to radius and permittivity.

Existing equivalent: use the same objective, but select the already available lazy namespace before evaluating it:

tr = tr.advect
value, gradient = ad.value_and_grad(scattering)(np.array([0.2, 3.0]))

This requires the installed Advect extra, but no import treams_rs.advect statement. It remains explicit backend selection.

Automatic selection would preserve the current adapter limits:

Adapter Current supported boundary
Advect CPU, first-order reverse mode; float32/64 and complex64/128 inputs, double-precision outputs. No forward mode, higher derivatives, staging or checkpointing. Source
JAX CPU, float64/complex128 with x64 enabled; reverse mode, JIT and sequential vmap. Backward reruns the Rust forward. No higher derivatives or forward mode. Return arrays across JIT boundaries, not physics objects. Adapter, object limitation
PyTorch CPU float64/complex128, eager autograd and repeated backward. No higher derivatives, forward mode, torch.func or torch.compile. Source

JAX callbacks need custom derivative rules; PyTorch compilation would need additional integration at the native-operation boundary. Neither follows from type dispatch. JAX callbacks, PyTorch custom operators

Bounded follow-up

Implementation should touch the selected root factory entry points, one small selection helper, and constant-wave promotion at the framework composition boundary. Reuse _framework.Constructors, existing backend objects and derivative bridges; no Rust derivative changes are indicated.

Validation should cover:

  1. Root-dispatched versus explicit-adapter values and gradients for radius, frequency and permittivity, including JAX JIT and PyTorch eager execution.
  2. Constant illumination, material tuples, nested inputs, mixed-backend rejection and documented unsupported constructors.
  3. Existing complex-gradient conventions: native dL = Re(vdot(g, dx)); JAX conjugates incoming and outgoing gradients, while Advect/PyTorch do not. Preserve scalar/flat-tuple outputs, input gradient shapes/dtypes, real-input projection and context lifetime. Shared contract
  4. Finite-difference comparisons plus existing physical identities, including scattering scaling and lossless absorption. Existing tests
  5. Fresh-process import checks and small-call benchmarks: no optional imports for NumPy use, unchanged return types, and measured dispatch overhead.

Source and official documentation were inspected; numerical examples were not executed. The existing Advect environment contains NumPy and Advect but lacks treams-rs, JAX and PyTorch. Nothing was installed, built, edited, committed or pushed; no PRs, comments or release coordination were changed.

text: ok implement this fully so that it is as user friendly as possible. basically using advect or jax or torch should just work (if those things are installed). users should not have to worry about it. and make sure we have the proper abstractions so this isnt a maintenance nightmare. while you’re at it, also add hips/autograd as an autodiff backend. this is on top of the release branch

items.html:
Implemented in treams-rs-autodiff, on feat/transparent-autodiff, based on release commit d472a003e22b.

Ordinary treams_rs calls now select Advect, JAX, PyTorch, or HIPS Autograd automatically. Imports stay lazy; all four reuse shared physics classes and native analytic derivatives.

import jax
import treams_rs as tr

def scattering(radius):
    return tr.sphere_tmatrix(
        k0=1.3, lmax=2, radius=radius, material=3
    ).xs_sca_avg

gradient = jax.jit(jax.grad(scattering))(0.2)

Documentation and examples for all four frameworks.

Verified:

  • 6,437 Python tests passed, 22 expected skips; lint, types, and documentation checks passed.
  • Clean wheel installations passed for NumPy, Advect, Autograd, and HDF5.
  • Rust: 240 tests passed; one unchanged baseline test fails under the required one-thread budget.

Limits remain CPU and first-order gradients; PyTorch compilation is unsupported. Numerical functions now use callable wrappers, changing literal np.ufunc identity. Small NumPy calls with frameworks loaded add roughly 2.5–12 µs, exceeding the microbenchmark’s overhead target.

Changes are local and uncommitted. Nothing pushed; no PR created; release worktree untouched.
